extracted.intended_audience: film and television production practitioners, students, and researchers (directors, camera operators, producers, cinematographers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive standards for planning and executing a multiple-camera (multicam) method in film, television and video production, including technical, creative, and logistical considerations. Covers roles of cameras, synchronization, typical uses, advantages, and drawbacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Camera roles and placement (outer cameras and master shot)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally, the two outer cameras shoot close-up shots or 'crosses' of the two most active characters on the set at any given time, while the central camera or cameras shoot a wider master shot to capture the overall action and establish the geography of the room.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This arrangement obtains multiple shot types in a single take without restarting the action; use outer cameras for character coverage and center camera(s) for the establishing/master coverage. Arrange coverage so the master defines spatial geography and the others supply reaction/close detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficiency and production speed
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple shots are obtained in a single take without having to start and stop the action; this is more efficient for programs that are to be shown a short time after being shot and is a virtual necessity for regular, high-output shows like daily soap operas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer multicam when turnaround time is short or output volume is high. The method reduces editing time and the need for re-lighting and reset between setups, enabling much faster scene throughput than single-camera methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lighting trade-offs and compromises
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawbacks include a less optimized lighting setup that needs to provide a compromise for all camera angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect to design lighting that works acceptably for all cameras rather than optimizing per shot; accept that lighting may be inferior to single-camera setups and plan accordingly (e.g., fewer dramatic lighting changes, more even high-key illumination for sitcoms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equipment placement and concealment constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Less flexibility in putting necessary equipment on scene, such as microphone booms and lighting rigs — these can be efficiently hidden from just one camera, but are more complicated to set up for multiple cameras.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan set and rigging to avoid visible equipment on any camera angle; consider camera positions when placing booms/stands and design blocking to minimize visible apparatus. Single-camera can hide equipment more easily; multicam requires more careful rigging or compromises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recording capacity / media usage
rubrics_metrics.description: A four-camera setup may use (depending on the cameras involved) up to four times as much film (or digital storage space) per take compared with a single-camera setup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Budget for increased film or storage needs and data-management workflows when using multiple cameras; consider ISO recording policies and long-take storage requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synchronization requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A multiple-camera setup will require all cameras to be synchronous to assist with editing and to avoid cameras running at different scan rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use SMPTE timecode or Genlock (primary methods mentioned) to sync cameras. Proper synchronization is essential for accurate switching, editing, and avoiding technical mismatches between camera feeds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director's live switching / line cut procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: In multiple-camera television, the director creates a line cut by instructing the technical director (vision mixer in UK terminology) to switch between the feeds from the individual cameras; this is either transmitted live or recorded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design workflow for either live transmission or recording the line cut. Ensure communication between director and technical director/vision mixer is reliable; train operators in live switching conventions. For studio audiences, display the line cut on monitors for immediate feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: ISO (individual camera) recording and later refinement
rubrics_metrics.description: Often the output from all cameras is recorded, both separately and as a combined reference display called the q split (a technique known as 'ISO' recording). The line cut might be refined later in editing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record all camera feeds individually (ISO) even if switching live; this allows postproduction refinements, alternate edits, and recovery from live-switching mistakes. Implement clear labeling and logging of ISO feeds for efficient postproduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of tally lights and camera signaling
rubrics_metrics.description: The camera currently being recorded to the line cut is indicated by a tally light controlled by a camera control unit (CCU) on the camera as a reference both for the talent and the camera operators, and an additional tally light may be used to indicate to the camera operator that they are being ISO recorded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure tally systems are functioning and understood by talent and operators. Use separate tally indicators when broadcasting vs ISO-recording to avoid confusion about which feed is live.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical camera counts and the 'fourth/X/D camera' norm
rubrics_metrics.description: Soon after the fourth camera (known then as the 'X' Camera, and occasionally today known as the 'D' Camera) was added for productions like Mork & Mindy, many productions followed suit and now having four cameras (A, B, C and X/D) is the norm for multi-camera situation comedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan for at least three cameras plus an additional 'X/D' camera for improvisational actors or alternative coverage; adapt crew and switching plans to accommodate the common A/B/C/X designation scheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability by program type / domains of use
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple-camera is commonly used for light entertainment, sports events, news, soap operas, talk shows, game shows, variety shows, and some sitcoms, especially ones filmed before a live studio audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose multicam when shows require live coverage, audience interaction, chronological action, or rapid turnaround. Avoid multicam for productions that demand extensive location shooting, complex visual effects, or highly stylized single-shot cinematography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chronological performance and live-action capture
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple cameras can take different shots of a live situation as the action unfolds chronologically, and are suitable for shows which require a live audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multicam to capture events performed in sequence (theatre-like blocking) rather than repeated, out-of-order takes. For scripted drama that benefits from non-chronological shooting, consider single-camera methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director control vs cost trade-off
rubrics_metrics.description: The multiple-camera method gives the director less control over each shot but is faster and less expensive than a single-camera setup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh the need for precise shot composition, camera movement, and single-shot aesthetics against budget and schedule constraints. Use single-camera when maximal directorial control and specific cinematography are primary goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Script and production documentation differences
rubrics_metrics.description: A sitcom shot with a multiple-camera setup will require a different form of script from a single-camera setup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare multicam scripts formatted and annotated for live blocking, audience timing, and camera coverage (e.g., act breaks, beat lines for audience laughter). Coordinate script pages with camera diagrams and cue sheets for technical crew.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations for visual effects, location variety, and tight editing
rubrics_metrics.description: Single-camera productions enable tightly edited sequences, multiple locations and visual effects such as magical appearances and disappearances; multiple-camera productions are more simplified and have been compared to theatre work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the production requires complex VFX, many locations, or finely edited sequences, favor single-camera; use multicam principally for studio-bound, performance-driven content with limited VFX demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity management benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Using multiple cameras reduces the complexity of tracking continuity issues that crop up when the scene is reshot from different angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit multicam to maintain continuous performance and reduce continuity errors between alternate takes; when continuity-sensitive moments are crucial, prefer multicam or ensure robust continuity logging.
